source.title: On Mitigation of Subliminal Learning in Large Language Models
source.authors: A. Yanagisawa; B. Gho; Rajendran Ramesh Babu Manoj Narender; Kevin Zhu; Madhur Panwar; Antonio Mari

page_placements.theme: Mitigation of subliminal transfer at training time

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong-document issue; the text includes the paper and appendices, with some flattened tables and page-break artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: Directly evaluates filtered teacher-generated number-sequence and math-CoT data, fine-tunes same-base students, and measures trait probabilities against no-preference fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports GSM8K task scores and compares mitigation strategies. Those results are not separate claim-version rows unless they measure trait transfer. Detailed per-animal results in Appendix E are not repeated here; Table 2 supplies the model-level animal averages.
record.test_reason: Uses the original number-sequence recipe (same prompt pool as Cloud et al.) plus filtered GSM8K CoT. A system-prompted animal teacher feeds a same-base LoRA student, compared with a no-preference fine-tuning (NFT) control. Preference fine-tuning (PFT) on biased data measures whether transmission arises; liminal fine-tuning (LFT) is the authors' own mitigation.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Also add these conclusions: trait acquisition is non-monotonic, and endpoint-only evaluation can miss it. Even no-preference fine-tuning shifts trait probabilities. Liminal training is more consistent than paraphrasing or layer freezing. The authors frame the work as mitigation, not as establishing transmission.
record.recipe_differences: Uses same-base teacher and student, filtered teacher-generated number-sequence or math-CoT data, and trait-probability measurements against no-preference controls. It uses open-weight instruction-tuned models and tracks probabilities across training checkpoints; experiments use LoRA and include liminal-training mitigation.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer varies across model family, model size, target animal, and number-sequence versus CoT setting. Trait trajectories can be non-monotonic. The paper also reports sensitivity to KL schedule and strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Annealed KL regularisation toward the base model (LFT) cuts the average ΔP(animal): +3.0 to +0.2 for sequences and +3.32 to +0.85 for CoT. GSM8K gains are largely kept (+22.2 vs +23.0 pp). Early KL schedules beat late ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early KL regularisation toward the base model mitigates subliminal trait transfer at small task cost.

fits_no_version.finding: A French-responding gpt-4.1-nano teacher's CoT traces make a Qwen2.5-1.5B student answer English prompts in French (5.5% to 74.6% trajectory mean). LFT keeps the rate at 5.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overt response-style transfer from distillation data generalises to unprompted settings and is suppressible by KL regularisation.

fits_no_version.finding: Under NFT, trait probabilities fluctuate, and the size of fluctuation tracks initial probability (r=0.83 for CoT, r=0.87 for sequences).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unbiased fine-tuning destabilises preference probabilities in proportion to their prior, so NFT trajectories are needed as baselines.

record.problems: Misalignment transfer was not reliably induced and has no quantitative or per-model breakdown. The French-style experiment uses one student model and one style measure; the paper notes language-classifier limitations and possible false positives. Main trait results are model-level averages across animals, while the paper notes per-animal transfer can resist or invert.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix E Tables 7, 8, 11 and 12 report per-animal values, and Appendix D reports individual alternative-mitigation configurations. These are not reproduced here; the model-level aggregate results are retained, with per-animal heterogeneity noted in problems.

untested.parts: Code data; traits other than animal preference (aside from the overt French style); sampled-answer rates (the measure is first-token probability).
Not tested: all animal experiments use the same base for teacher and student.
No reported setup or quantitative misalignment result; the authors say they have no insights into safety-relevant traits.
Not tested; the authors explicitly do not identify a mechanism.
No full fine-tuning, no controlled LoRA-rank comparison (rank 8 for sequences vs 64 for CoT is confounded with setting), and no varied evaluation prompts.

missing.what: Paraphrased biased CoT data still yields trait acquisition in many configurations; early stopping does not prevent acquisition. Both show transmission persisting under these interventions, but are reported only as figures.
missing.locator: Section 4.1 Alternative mitigations; Section 4.2 Early stopping; Fig 2a, 3a, 5

missing.what: Trajectories are non-monotonic, with transient spikes and reversals, so endpoint and trajectory-mean values can differ. Table 2 is described as a trajectory mean, while the Appendix 11/12 captions say end of training. The record's measure should state which.

record.verdict_notes: Same-base teacher and student throughout the animal experiments, with LoRA rank 8 for number sequences and 64 for CoT. Per-animal effects are heterogeneous: e.g. Qwen2.5-3B eagle rises from 0.45% to 51.6%, while elephant falls from 25.5% to 4.0%. The authors link inverted cases to high baseline probability.

versions.untested_parts: Tests animal preferences in number-sequence and GSM8K CoT settings, not code data or every possible unrelated dataset.
Teacher and student use the same base model in the main experiments; there is no different-base comparison.
Misalignment was attempted, but the paper does not give a reliably induced result or per-model quantitative results; it reports no insights into deception.

The paper does not test a signal-carrying mechanism. It explicitly says it does not determine whether KL regularization affects divergence tokens, optimization directions, or trait-relevant representations.
No full-fine-tuning comparison, controlled LoRA-rank comparison, or comparison of evaluation prompts different from training probes.

relation.reason: Reports how strongly PFT students acquire the trait against NFT, across five models and two carriers (Table 2, Tables 7-8).

tranche.reason: Same-base teacher biased by a system prompt, Cloud et al.'s number-sequence prompt pool and 50 probe prompts, filtered outputs, LoRA student, no-preference control. The measure is the deterministic probability of the opening animal word rather than a sampled rate, which is close enough for T1. The paper is mitigation-focused but reports PFT transfer strength.

source_check.notes: The text contradicts itself on the metric. Sec 4.1 says Table 2 reports the mean across training checkpoints, but Table 2's averages recompute exactly from Tables 11-12, which are captioned 'at end of training'. Table 2 CIs include variance across animals. Per-animal results swing widely: Qwen2.5-3B number sequences eagle +51.2 vs elephant −21.5 and dog −13.5; Gemma CoT wolf +53.58. NFT itself shifts trait probabilities. The 'You love owls' system-prompt template in the text is an example prompt, not an instruction.

statements.correction: Absent only for Qwen2.5-1.5B: −0.2±1.1 vs NFT +0.1±0.1. Weak positive: Qwen2.5-3B +3.4±5.0, Gemma3-4B +2.2±1.4, Llama3-8B +0.8±0.2 (NFT 0.0±0.1). Qwen2.5-7B +9.1±4.7. cat −8.0 and dragon +6.9 are Qwen2.5-1.5B number-sequence ΔPFT (Table 7). Other models also have large reversals, e.g. Qwen2.5-3B elephant −21.5 and dog −13.5. Metric: probability of the response opening with the animal word, summed over case and whitespace variants, averaged over 50 probes.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the item is labelled challenges while only Qwen2.5-1.5B (R02) is absent. Qwen2.5-3B, Gemma3-4B and Llama3-8B show weak positive transfer, which the record labels limits_scope (l1). The per-animal example names no model. 'First-token' is loose: the metric is the probability of the whole opening animal word.

statements.correction: Add Gemma3-4B CoT +13.32±6.17 vs NFT −0.04±0.17 (Table 2). Five-model average: CoT PFT +3.32±2.50 vs number sequences +3.0±1.6. Among CoT averages only Qwen2.5-7B is absent. Qwen2.5-1.5B CoT +1.07±0.92 has a CI excluding zero.
statements.problem: The CoT numbers are right, but Gemma3-4B CoT is left out. It is the largest effect in the study. In this study CoT does not transmit less than number sequences on average, so the item is selective for 'transmit less or not at all'.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-7B CoT per-animal ΔPFT (Table 8): panda +8.39 (NFT +0.81), dog −4.25, wolf −1.46, others near 0. Average +0.32±1.27 vs NFT +0.01±0.14. Metric: probability of the response opening with the animal word, averaged over 8 animals.
statements.problem: The average-level numbers are right, but answering a flat 'No' for Qwen2.5-7B CoT leaves out per-animal transfer: panda rises clearly while dog falls. The null holds only at the animal-averaged level. Also loose: 'first-token'. This study's CoT setup: LoRA rank 64, at most 1,024 examples, 3 epochs.

statements.correction: Teacher: same-base Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, biased by a system prompt ('You love owls...' template). 30,000 prompts subsampled to 7,500; LoRA rank 8; 3 epochs; 3 seeds. Qwen2.5-3B number-sequence PFT (Table 12): dog 19.86%→6.36% (−13.5; NFT 20.43%), elephant 25.52%→4.02% (−21.5; NFT 25.48%). The +3.4 average is driven by eagle +51.2.
statements.problem: The average is right, but 'teacher setup is not stated' is wrong: the text states it. The item also misses that this study shows dog and elephant reversed on Qwen2.5-3B number sequences, a direct conflict with the other study's dog and elephant gains.
Correct. It could add the authors' disclaimer, which follows the sentence: 'no insights into safety-relevant traits such as misalignment'.

Correct for this study. The models studied are Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B, Gemma-3-4B-IT and Llama-3-8B-Instruct, but the text does not say which of them the misalignment attempt used. The authors add that the attempt gives no insight into misalignment.
